jobs.title: THIS Triad System Will 13X Your RHYTHM Guitar Playing
jobs.lessonTitle: Building the chords of any key
jobs.stepTitle: The whole key in one 5-fret window
jobs.prompt:
You are helping a guitar teacher fit a YouTube lesson video into a written lesson. Watch the whole video and listen to what the teacher says and plays.

Lesson: "Building the chords of any key" (Level 2, lesson 6).
Goal: Build the seven chords of any major key by stacking 3rds, know the major-minor-minor-major-major-minor-diminished pattern, use Roman numerals and Nashville numbers, and play the common progressions in any key.
Learn sections: "Stack 3rds on every note", "The pattern for every major key", "Three pairs and an odd one", "The progressions everyone uses", "The key on the neck: a box of roots (CAGED)", "The whole key in one 5-fret window".
The text of the step the video is in ("The whole key in one 5-fret window"):
Barre chords move your hand all over the neck. Rhythm players often do the opposite: they play the key's chords as small three-string triads and keep them all inside one 5-fret window. In C major, on the D, G and B strings, frets 5 to 9, all seven chords fit:
- C (I): 5-5-5 on D-G-B (xx555x)
- Dm (ii): 7-7-6 (xx776x)
- Em (iii): 9-9-8 (xx998x)
- F (IV): 7-5-6 (xx756x): index finger flat across
- G (V): 9-7-8 (xx978x): the same shape as F, two frets up
- Am (vi): 7-5-5 (xx755x)
- B° (vii°): 9-7-6 (xx976x): a little stretch
Why it sounds so good: from one chord to the next, each finger moves a fret or two at most, often not at all. Each note slides to the nearest note of the next chord. That's voice leading: the parts stay connected, the guitar sits neatly in a band above the bass and the keys, and it sounds like a record instead of a strum-along.
Make them move: a triad on its own can sound static. Add the scale note just above one of its notes and fall back, with a hammer-on, pull-off or slide: on C (G C E), the A above G, the D above C, or the F above E. That one note turns a block chord into a rhythm part.
Tip: Practise it the additive way: C → Dm until it's easy, then C → Dm → Em, then add one chord at a time, always over a drum beat so the changes land in time. (On ukulele the app finds the closest-moving shapes for your tuning.)

jobs.lessonTitle: CAGED: the map of the whole neck
jobs.stepTitle: 2 · Making them movable: the nut becomes a finger
jobs.prompt:
You are helping a guitar teacher fit a YouTube lesson video into a written lesson. Watch the whole video and listen to what the teacher says and plays.

Lesson: "CAGED: the map of the whole neck" (Level 4, lesson 1).
Goal: Play any major or minor chord in all five shapes, know where the root, 3rd and 5th are in each, move through a key without leaving one area of the neck, and use the shapes as the frame for scales, arpeggios, triads and fills.
Learn sections: "1 · Five chords you already know", "2 · Making them movable: the nut becomes a finger", "3 · Why the shapes look the way they do (the B-string kink)", "4 · One chord, five places: C up the neck", "5 · The glue: how each shape hands over to the next", "6 · Any chord, anywhere: the root finders", "7 · Where the 1, 3 and 5 are in every shape", "8 · Minor chords in five shapes", "9 · The grips players actually use", "10 · Scales and arpeggios live inside the shapes", "11 · One key, five zones: change chords without moving", "12 · The three directions: how mastery is built", "13 · Finding any note with the shape around it", "14 · CAGED in real music", "15 · What mastery looks like".
The text of the step the video is in ("2 · Making them movable: the nut becomes a finger"):
An open chord leans on the nut: the open strings are notes the nut "frets" for you. To move a shape up the neck, something has to do the nut's job. That's your index finger: a barre, or just a finger on the notes that were open.
You already know two cases. F at the 1st fret is the E shape with the index finger as the nut. B♭ at the 1st fret is the A shape. Slide either one up, and the chord's name is simply the note under the root: E shape at the 5th fret = A (low E string, 5th fret is A); A shape at the 5th fret = D (A string, 5th fret is D).
The other three work the same way, they are just less comfortable as full barres:
- C shape moved up: the index finger takes the open G and E strings; the root is under the ring finger on the A string, three frets above the index.
- G shape moved up: the index takes the open D, G and B strings; roots under the ring or little finger on the low and high E strings.
- D shape moved up: the index takes the open D string root; the shape sits ahead of it, two or three frets up.
Tip: Shape and name are two different things. "C shape" says which pattern; the chord's name comes from the root under it. A D chord can be played with the C shape, the A shape, the G shape, the E shape or the D shape.

A triad is three notes: the root, the 3rd and the 5th. On three neighbouring strings you play each note once, and there are only three ways to stack them, named after the lowest note:
- Root position: the root at the bottom (R – 3 – 5). The 5th is on top.
- 1st inversion: the 3rd at the bottom (3 – 5 – R). The root is on top.
- 2nd inversion: the 5th at the bottom (5 – R – 3). The 3rd is on top.

- Root position: 5 5 3.

The text of the step the video is in ("6 · Spread triads: the big open sound"):
A close triad fits inside an octave. A spread (or open) triad takes the middle note and moves it up an octave, so the chord stretches over more than an octave. On guitar that means skipping a string between the bottom two notes:
- R-5-3 (root at the bottom): C on E-D-G = 8 10 9. On D-B-e = 10 8 12.
- 3-R-5 (3rd at the bottom): C on E-D-G = 12 10 12. On A-G-B = 7 5 8.
- 5-3-R (5th at the bottom): C on E-D-G = 3 2 5. On A-G-B = 10 9 13.
Why it sounds so good: the notes are far enough apart that none of them rub, and the 3rd sits high where it sings. Piano players call it an open voicing; string sections and choirs use it all the time. Played fingerstyle (thumb on the low note, two fingers on the others) it's instant cinematic guitar.
Mute the skipped string with the underside of the finger on the lower note, or pick with fingers so it never sounds.

jobs.prompt:

Lesson: "Rhythm 4: sixteenths and syncopation" (Level 4, lesson 8).
Goal: Count and play sixteenth notes, keep the strumming hand moving in sixteenths while choosing which strokes hit, use ghost strums and accents for funk grooves, and play syncopated rhythms and anticipated chord changes in time.
Learn sections: "1 · Counting sixteenths", "2 · The strumming hand as a sixteenth motor", "3 · Ghost strums, muting and accents", "4 · Syncopation and anticipation", "5 · Where you'll hear it", "6 · What mastery looks like".
The text of the step the video is in ("2 · The strumming hand as a sixteenth motor"):
The secret of sixteenth strumming: the hand never stops. It moves down on 1 and &, up on e and a, every beat, like a pendulum. The rhythm comes from whether the pick hits the strings or misses them on each stroke.
- Downstrokes always land on the 1 e & a grid's "1" and "&"; upstrokes on "e" and "a".
- If a rhythm has a note on the "a", it's an upstroke. If it starts on the "e", it's an upstroke too.
- Missing strokes: keep the motion, just move the pick slightly away from the strings.
Because the motion is constant, your timing is locked to it: you can't rush a note that the hand isn't ready to play. That's why funk players can play such tight, complicated rhythms.

The text of the step the video is in ("5 · Augmented: symmetry, V+ and the line cliché"):
An augmented triad is two major 3rds: C to E to G♯, and G♯ to C is another major 3rd. It's symmetrical too: move it up 4 frets and you have the same three notes. C+ = E+ = G♯+, so there are only four augmented triads in all.

- V+ → I: play G+ (G B D♯) instead of G before C. The D♯ pushes up to E, the 3rd of C.
- The line cliché: hold a chord and move one inner voice up by half steps. C – C+ – C6 – C7: the 5th goes G, G♯, A, B♭, then lands on F. It's the sound of a film score or a lounge ballad slowly opening up.
- III+ in a minor key: harmonic minor (lesson 6 and Level 7) builds an augmented chord on its 3rd degree (C+ in A minor).
Tip: You don't need many shapes. One augmented shape and one dim7 shape, slid up the neck by 4 and 3 frets, cover every one of these chords.
